Subject: Question on billing math for commit/discount phasing

Sergio —

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Two procurement questions came up as we evaluate the reserved-commit package you quoted: how you apply token rounding/minimums across mixed workloads, and how discounts phase in as committed units grow over a quarter. I attached a short sample of our usage patterns (usage_sample_Q3.csv) — it shows a mix of short interactive calls (~120 tokens) and very long batch requests (45k tokens) that we run intermittently.

Specific asks:
- If we commit 5M tokens/month with a 10% discount, and then spike on a batch that consumes 45M tokens on a single day, do you charge the batch against the commit at the same unit granularity or is there a different treatment for long-context inference?
- How do you round partial billing units? Your team mentioned a 1k-token increment; does that apply per-request, per-session, or at invoice aggregation?
- If we step up our commit mid-quarter (e.g., 5M -> 10M), does the discount apply pro rata for the remainder of the quarter or do you apply retrospective credits?

If it's easier, we can jump on a quick call — procurement is on a tight timeline for our Q1 budget.

—Oliver

Head of AI Product, NovaCorp

From: sergio_alvarez@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Question on billing math for commit/discount phasing

Hi Oliver — appreciate the sample, that helps. I pulled together the answers and a short example workbook (redwood_example_calcs.xlsx) — attaching and summarizing below so procurement has something concrete to pass to finance.

Short answers up front:
1) Long-batch vs interactive: we bill identical unit types for both (tokens), but we treat very long single-request contexts as two things for operational clarity: (a) the tokens are counted to the same token-meter that determines consumption, and (b) for high context lengths > model native limit we may route to a batch-optimized model variant that uses a different GPU kernel. Pricing unit stays token-based. There is no separate "batch surcharge" — cost differences are reflected in the model variant and therefore the per-token rate.

2) Rounding: our billing is applied in 1,000-token increments. Rounding is done at the invoice-window aggregation level, not per-message. Implementation details: within a billing window (monthly) we sum raw tokens across all requests, then divide by 1,000 and round up to the nearest whole increment. Example: total tokens = 5,012,320 -> billed units = ceil(5,012.320) = 5,013 (thousands) -> billed tokens = 5,013,000. This avoids per-request over-rounding for many tiny calls.

3) Mid-quarter commit increases: we apply the new commitment pro rata for the remainder of the billing period. We do not retroactively credit previous usage unless we agreed to a retrospective true-up in the contract. If you'd like retrospective crediting, we can include a clause that applies a one-time catch-up credit on a quarterly true-up (common in enterprise deals).

Example scenario (see workbook):
- Committed: 5,000k tokens/month at $0.0025 per token (10% off list)
- Usage month: regular interactive + one 45M-token batch day -> total tokens = 50,120,000
- Billed units (1k increments): ceil(50,120) = 50,120 -> billed tokens = 50,120,000
- Charge before discount = 50,120,000 * $0.0025 = $125,300
- Commit credit: we apply the 5,000k commit at the committed discounted rate, then bill overage at list or an overage tier per contract. How we apply commit vs overage is negotiable — typical approach: commit covers first 5,000k at discounted rate; remaining charged at overage rate ($0.003 per token or tiered).

Proposed flexible option: to avoid large one-day charge disruptions we can add a burst buffer for the quarter (one-time buffer equal to X% of commit) that gets amortized. For example, a 400% burst buffer on a 5M commit would absorb a 20M spike without immediate overage; excess is amortized over subsequent months or billed per the overage tier.

Next steps I'd propose:
- I've attached an example workbook with per-line math and three variants (standard rounding, per-request rounding, and with a burst buffer).
- If NovaCorp prefers more predictable overage treatment, we can draft contract language for a quarterly true-up or a burst buffer.

Happy to walk through the workbook on a short call. When are you free this week?

—Sergio
Sergio Alvarez
Enterprise Accounts | Redwood Inference

One ask: can you provide a canned invoice example that shows a) the commit credit being applied, b) the overage calculation, and c) the rounded invoice line items? I'll try to collect a representative spike pattern for you if that helps; otherwise let's schedule time to review the workbook and a sample invoice. We're available Thursday 10–11am PT.

Oliver — looping in finance & billing. Short answers to procurement asks: yes, we can provide a mock invoice showing commit credit application, overage lines, and rounding math. We'll generate two variants: one with a burst buffer amortized across the quarter, and one with a true-up credit line. 

Operational notes:
- Amortization approach: we create a quarterly amortization line that spreads the buffer allowance evenly over the remaining invoice periods in the quarter. That line will appear as a negative amortization credit each month until fully applied. This requires no manual reconciliation on NovaCorp's side beyond typical invoice matching.
- A one-time system flag is required if you want retrospective credits; otherwise behavior is forward-looking (pro rata).

I'll have a mock invoice & amortization schedule ready by Wednesday EOD. I can also draft SOW language for the burst buffer/quarterly true-up if procurement wants explicit contract text.
